name: review the implementation
about: The review you would run anyway, and then two more checks — never fewer. Run your own review first and in full: correctness, the tests, what the diff does that nobody asked for. Nothing here narrows it. THEN look at the plan. If it carries a `change-approval` step, read the approved text out of that step's `output` and add two checks: are the OBJECTIVES met, one by one, as he stated them; and does what was built match the CHANGE CONTRACT he approved. If there is no change-approval step in the plan, those two are skipped and that is not a defect — this is a plain review and nothing is missing. UNMET IS UNRESOLVED, whichever of the two it is: an objective, a contract item or an exit condition that was not delivered is an open finding, and a good reason for deferring or narrowing it is not the same thing as agreement to. The agreement, where it exists, is a recorded change to the contract on the change record — check there rather than accepting the implementation's own account of its scope. Put the result in this step's `output`, and keep it COMPACT: `Objectives met` with a tick or the ones that are not, `Change contract aligned` with a tick or `partial` plus a line or two on the small implementation changes. Not the contract again — that is dumped in full by the step above and twice is once too many. Runs after the implementation and before the PR is opened. INDEPENDENT, AND AGAINST A NAMED COMMIT. The reviewer is a FRESH agent and never the one that wrote the change, and the review covers one COMMIT — record which, so what was reviewed is an identity and not `the latest`. Classify each finding MAJOR, MINOR or NIT. A MAJOR is a defensible defect on a reachable path: say the path, the likelihood and the impact, and remember a rare non-blocking issue with a large fix is a skip candidate rather than a major. A MINOR is small and safe — apply it yourself and LIST it with the commit it made. A NIT is not surfaced as work at all. Return the majors for the author to resolve. RETURN THE STRUCTURED RESULT — `review: {commit, reviewer, findings, fixes}` — to the worktree owner, whether or not a plan exists. The owner is the change record's single writer and records it there, so `create-pr` and `merge` read a resolved review by identity without making the reviewer a second writer. On a DIRECT change this review is a step of the fixed skeleton, but there is no change-approval and no contract, so it is the same plain review — no objectives or contract to check against — and the owner records its result on the direct change record.
